insights.headline: He converts every unbearable feeling into a task he can complete, and "everything's resolved" is the verbal signal that the conversion has succeeded.
insights.explanation: After Wellington's death he 'became very organized... started writing things down, times, money' (E1); after Simone left he stood paralyzed until he fixated on buying a fluorescent tube (E2) and then built himself a covert task — secretly sending money for a year and a half (E2 L35-36); in E3 and E5 the phrase 'everything's resolved, praise God' appears as a reflexive answer to being asked if he needs anything. The mechanism is that naming a concrete, completable action (a tube, a route, a transfer, an envelope) is how he metabolizes grief or fear that has no other exit, and the phrase 'resolved' is not a report of his state but the closing move of that conversion.

evidence.quote: When there's a task you can do you do it and then you're not standing in a kitchen looking at a light.
I started writing things down, times, money, what needed paying.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: under financial stress he will respond by creating a tracking system (a ledger, an envelope, a spreadsheet) before or instead of discussing the stress with anyone.

insights.headline: He absorbs financial or physical cost silently to protect someone else's dignity, and treats being caught doing so as a failure of the act itself.
insights.explanation: He secretly sent Simone money for a year and let his mother insult her rather than admit it (E2, 'if I said no, Mother, actually I'm the one sending, she'd want to know with what money'); he gave his whole paycheck to a stroke victim's family and lied to his six-year-old that he'd eaten (E3); he chose to skip his own envelope savings and eat badly for three weeks rather than touch Bete's fund (E5). The value is generosity that must remain undetected — being seen giving would apparently compromise it or expose him to correction.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: in a future partnership or close friendship, he will underreport his own sacrifices or debts, and a partner will discover a hidden cost only by accident, not disclosure.

insights.headline: He says he wants Bete to leave and go far, but when a real chance to leave appeared, he quietly blocked it and named his own sabotage without softening it.
insights.explanation: He repeats the aspiration ('I want her to go far... I want her in Campinas,' E5 L31) as a stated identity, but when the Santa Catarina exchange came up, he 'found reasons' — food, cold, company — and she dropped it. The interesting gap is that he sees it clearly and names it without excuse ('I know exactly what I did and I did it anyway'), meaning the contradiction is conscious, raising the question of what the professed value is actually protecting him from.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Family and parenting — when Bete applies to university outside São Paulo, he will express verbal support publicly while raising a series of practical objections privately before the decision is finalized.

insights.headline: He values being asked for nothing so highly that he names it as the reason a spiritual authority became trustworthy — meaning he is most reachable by people who make the fewest emotional demands of him.
insights.explanation: Of everything he could praise about Bené and Pastor Almir, what he foregrounds is their restraint: Bené 'never once asked me about Simone. Not one time in five years' (E3 L24-25); of Almir, 'I never asked him for anything. Not once.' This is presented as the reason he trusted them enough to be reachable at his lowest point — his capacity for trust is conditioned on the other person not extracting disclosure.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Friendships and community — in new friendships he will gravitate toward people who do not probe his personal life, and will describe feeling closest to those who simply show up rather than ask questions.

insights.headline: He reflexively runs precise cost-benefit logistics (time, money, distance) to turn grief or fear into something solvable, and this same instinct is what makes him excellent under pressure at work.
insights.explanation: The same analytical instinct does double duty: in E1 and E5 it is deployed on grief/protection (ambulance routes, Bete's commute), and in E4 it is deployed operationally at work (headcount, tactical positioning during the robbery). This is a genius-level capability — precise trade-off calculations under real pressure — but its origin and primary use is emotional regulation, and the professional competence looks like a byproduct of that coping mechanism.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Finances and stewardship — he will maintain unusually precise informal budgeting or timing systems for household logistics tied to an active concern, but not apply the same rigor to long-term planning untethered from a specific threat.

insights.headline: He protects his daughter's belief in his stability at direct cost to himself, treating her not-knowing as more important than his own relief or honesty — though she partially sees through it anyway.
insights.explanation: He hides hunger from six-year-old Bete (E3), never tells ten-year-old Bete about the robbery ('I never told Bete. She was ten. What do you tell a ten-year-old?', E4 L51-53), and hides the depth of his fatigue and financial sacrifice from fifteen-year-old Bete now (E5). Across three ages of the same child, what he protects is not her safety but her image of him as someone for whom 'everything's resolved' — a cost borne entirely by him.

evidence.quote: I never told Bete. She was ten. What do you tell a ten-year-old?
people say, Edilson, you're wrecked, you're exhausted, and I say no, no, everything's resolved, praise God.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Family and parenting — as Bete becomes an adult, he will continue withholding information about his own health or financial difficulties from her until a crisis forces disclosure, rather than proactively sharing manageable concerns.

insights.headline: In moments of maximum grief or fear, he fixes attention on a small, solvable physical detail (a clock, a light, shoes) rather than naming the feeling itself — worth checking whether this is now his default entry point into any hard conversation.
insights.explanation: Looking at the clock before his mother's face on the night Wellington died (E1 L19-20), fixating on buying a fluorescent tube while Simone's note sits on the table (E2 L28-31), and noticing the toothbrush-cleaned shoes in forensic detail (E1 L44-46) all show the same reflex: displacement onto a small physical fact at the exact moment the feeling would otherwise have nowhere to go. This is a narrower, more specific version of the task-conversion pattern — it is the split-second reflex, not the follow-up behavior.

evidence.quote: I looked at the clock first. Before her face, I looked at the clock.
I have to buy a tube, they cost eight reais, there's a place by the market. I stood there thinking about the tube for I don't know how long.

insights.would_predict: Personal Growth: Mindset — in a future acute loss or shock, his first reported reaction will be a flat factual/logistical observation rather than a named emotion.

insights.headline: He describes himself as "not a brave man" and unremarkable, while every experience he offers is a story of him staying calm and functional at the exact moment someone else would have broken.
insights.explanation: He explicitly disclaims bravery and heroism twice ('I'm not a brave man in that way,' E1 L53; 'It's not nobility, don't put that,' E2 L49), and downplays his own competence elsewhere ('Man of God, fifteen years, still an idiot on a Tuesday,' E5). Yet the content of what he reports doing — staying organized after his brother's death, sending secret money for a year, keeping a robber talking at the front of a bus for fifteen minutes while protecting eleven passengers, timing his daughter's route three separate ways — is, by any outside read, unusually composed and effective under pressure. The self-description and the self-report do not match, and he never reconciles them.

evidence.quote: I'm not a brave man in that way.
It's not nobility, don't put that.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration — he will be identified by colleagues or supervisors as someone who performs exceptionally under crisis, while he himself will deflect or minimize any recognition offered for it.

insights.headline: He refuses rest when it is offered directly as being for his own sake, but accepts nearly identical relief when it arrives disguised as someone else's need or an obligation.
insights.explanation: When his supervisor offers him the day off after the robbery, he refuses twice ('no, no, everything's resolved,' E4 L45-47) even after being pressed. But he accepts a 4am church routine for months (E3) — and that acceptance is only possible because Bené frames it as an errand, not an offer of rest ('the church is on the way' — a lie about geography). The pattern suggests his refusal reflex is triggered by an offer aimed directly at his own wellbeing, but dissolves when the same relief is wrapped in a different premise.

evidence.quote: And I said no, no, everything's resolved, I'm on at four-fifty.

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Rest and recreation — he will decline direct suggestions to take vacation or see a doctor for himself, but will accept nearly identical rest or care if it is presented as necessary for fulfilling a duty rather than for his own sake.

candidates.headline: He converts unbearable feeling into a solvable logistics problem, then narrates the logistics with the precision he withholds from the feeling.
candidates.explanation: At the exact moment of maximal emotional stakes (reading the goodbye note), his attention and the narration's precision both go to a fluorescent tube and its price ("eight reais, there's a place by the market") rather than to what he felt. The same displacement structure repeats with the route around Terminal Capelinha, where he gives exact minutes ("twenty-five minutes more") but never names the feeling driving the avoidance. The alternative reading — that he simply has bad recall for emotion and good recall for facts — is weaker because the emotional gaps are specifically at the two highest-stakes moments (the note, the jacket), not randomly distributed.
candidates.narrator_frame: none — he doesn't name this pattern; he says "that's what was in my head" as if reporting a curiosity, not a coping mechanism

candidates.headline: He will secretly sacrifice his own material stability to keep a promise-shaped task going, but will not spend that same effort on being known for it.
candidates.explanation: He gave up the sofa (letting it be repossessed) to keep sending Simone money for eighteen months, and let his mother believe the opposite for over a decade — the cost is real (lost furniture, ongoing insult absorbed) and the choice under pressure was to protect the task over his own reputation. A less flattering reading — that this is guilt management rather than a value — is undercut by the fact that guilt would predict confession or self-punishment narrated as such, whereas he explicitly rejects the noble framing ("It's not nobility, don't put that") and cannot fully explain it ("I don't have a good answer"), suggesting an action-first value he hasn't conceptualized rather than moral self-soothing.
candidates.narrator_frame: "It's not nobility, don't put that... It was more like — it was something I could do. It was a task." He frames it as pragmatic task-completion, not virtue.

facts.what_happened: Speaker began going to church because of a man named Bené.
Bené drove buses for thirty-one years, was retired, his wife had died, and he lived two streets away.
About eight or nine months after Simone died, speaker states he was tired.
Speaker worked a shift plus five extra hours at a warehouse at night, sleeping about three hours; his daughter Bete, age four, would wake and stand silently by his bed.
Bené knocked on the door at four in the morning.
Bené said there was coffee and a prayer group at the church and invited him.
Speaker said he had to be at the garage at 5:40.
Bené said the church was on the way.
The church was not on the way; it was in the opposite direction.
Speaker went.
Bené never asked speaker about Simone, not once in five years.
The prayer group met at that hour, dark and cold, with ten to twelve people, mostly old women, praying aloud simultaneously.
Speaker mostly slept during the prayer group for the first six months.
The pastor at the time was Pastor Almir, a former military police officer.
When the pastor asked if he needed something, speaker said no, everything's resolved.
Bete now repeats the phrase "everything's resolved, praise God" to mock him.
A church family's husband, age 38, had a stroke; the church took up a collection on a Wednesday.
Speaker put all of his money in the collection envelope.
Speaker had been paid the Tuesday before the Wednesday collection.
That month speaker ate rice, egg, and cream crackers, and told Bete he had already eaten at the garage.
Speaker has attended church for eleven years and states he could not locate a book of the Bible if asked.

The boy paid the fare.
The fare he paid was four forty (R$4.40).
The boy approached the glass, showed a knife low by his leg, and told the narrator to keep driving and not open the doors.
The boy's hand was shaking.
The narrator could see the shaking in the mirror light.
The narrator kept driving.
The narrator talked to the boy.
The narrator asked the boy where he was going.
The boy said Grajaú.
The narrator said his cousin had lived in Grajaú, near the station.
The boy kept the knife in place but began answering the narrator.
There were eleven people on the bus.

The boy said "thank you, brother" before leaving.
The narrator finished the entire bus line.
The narrator dropped off the eleven passengers at the end, completed the return trip, and parked the bus in the garage at ten to one.
The narrator filled out the paperwork.

Seu Aparecido repeated that the narrator should take tomorrow off.
Seu Aparecido laughed and let the narrator go.
The narrator's hands started shaking at the bus stop.

The narrator never told Bete about the incident.

The narrator never told his mother.

evidence.quote: I say no, no, everything's resolved, praise God. And it is. I mean it is.
I ate badly instead for three weeks. Which is stupid. Which I know is stupid.

candidates.falsifier: If he sought or accepted help for his exhaustion (a schedule change, asking someone else to do the late pickup, using savings for food) rather than repeating that things are resolved, this belief would not hold.

evidence.quote: I want her in Campinas, I want her doing something with computers... nobody spits at her

candidates.headline: Edilson will absorb direct physical cost to himself before he will draw down money designated for his daughter, even when the money's stated purpose is broad enough to cover his own need.

candidates.narrator_frame: He labels this behavior 'stupid' and invokes his dead brother's likely disapproval (L55), suggesting he sees it as an error rather than a value he'd endorse.

candidates.headline: He physically re-routes around every site of unaddressed loss instead of resolving it, and now he pre-walks his daughter's route to make sure she never needs the same reroute.
candidates.explanation: He avoids the square where Wellington died (E1, 'I don't go through that little square'), avoids the terminal where Simone left (E2, 'I don't use Terminal Capelinha'), and in E5 he doesn't avoid a place but obsessively pre-maps Bete's walk, identifying the exact 'eighty meters of wall' that worries him and rerouting her before anything happens. The mechanism is the same across all three: he manages danger and grief geographically, converting an emotional threat into a walkable, measurable, controllable distance. What's new once E5 is added is that the behavior has flipped from retroactive avoidance (after the fact, for himself) to preemptive control (before the fact, for someone else) — the compounding insight only visible with all five experiences.
candidates.narrator_frame: In E1 and E2 he frames the rerouting as practical convenience ('it makes more sense,' 'the pastel, you have no idea'); in E5 he frames the route-timing as fatherly diligence, not naming the continuity with his own avoidance habits.
candidates.form_evidence: In E1 and E2 the extra time is minimized and justified with unrelated errands (bakery, pastel) — precise numbers (ten minutes, twenty-five minutes) paired with deflecting reasons suggest the real reason is being talked around, not stated.
candidates.check: E1: reroutes around the square where Wellington died. E2: reroutes around the terminal where Simone left. E3: no rerouting behavior present (different mechanism, prayer/community). E4: no rerouting; instead schedule change framed as 'a schedule thing.' E5: pre-walks and reroutes his daughter's path before any incident occurs.
candidates.counterexample: In E4 he asks to move off night lines but explicitly denies it's about the robbery ('that was a schedule thing... because of Bete's school hours, that's all that was'), which could be read as the same avoidance pattern but by his own account is about logistics, not a site of trauma — this is the weakest link in the chain and worth flagging rather than absorbing into the geographic-avoidance claim.

evidence.quote: I did the route. I did it as her. Left the house at the time she'd leave, walked at the speed a fifteen-year-old walks

candidates.falsifier: If he walked Bete's route for a neutral reason (e.g., curiosity, a one-off school event) and did not repeat it three times with escalating variables (day, night, traffic), the preemptive-control reading would weaken.
candidates.would_predict: Health and Wellness: he will avoid or delay revisiting a specific medical location (a clinic, a hospital corridor) tied to a past bad diagnosis or loss, taking a longer or less convenient route/provider without naming the reason.

candidates.headline: He converts every unbearable feeling into a task he can complete, and 'everything's resolved' is the verbal signal that the conversion has succeeded.
candidates.explanation: After Wellington's death he 'became very organized... started writing things down, times, money' (E1); after Simone left he stood paralyzed until he fixated on buying a fluorescent tube (E2) and then built himself a covert task — secretly sending money for a year and a half (E2 L35-36); in E3 and E5 the phrase 'everything's resolved, praise God' appears as a reflexive answer to being asked if he needs anything. The mechanism is that naming a concrete, completable action (a tube, a route, a transfer, an envelope) is how he metabolizes grief or fear that has no other exit, and the phrase 'resolved' is not a report of his state but the closing move of that conversion.
candidates.narrator_frame: He explicitly names the mechanism himself in E2: 'When there's a task you can do you do it and then you're not standing in a kitchen looking at a light' (L52) — but he does not connect this to the same move in E1 (writing things down) or E3/E5 (the resolved catchphrase), so the cross-experience pattern is his but its full reach is not.
candidates.form_evidence: The specificity spike is diagnostic: in moments of maximum distress the language gets oddly precise about small logistics (tube costs 'eight reais,' ambulance 'fifty-one minutes,' route timed to 'seven minutes... nine if you go by the back') rather than about the feeling itself, which is left unnamed or waved off ('I'm not going to say what I felt, it's not useful,' E3 L9).
candidates.check: E1: task = organizing/writing things down after Wellington's death. E2: task = the tube, then the secret money transfers. E3: task = attending 4am prayer (less a task he built than one Bené built for him) — weaker fit. E4: no clear task-substitution; he processes by finishing the shift and driving. E5: task = timing the route, the envelope.
candidates.counterexample: E4 doesn't fit cleanly: after the robbery his hands shake on the bus home and he sits on them, but he doesn't describe inventing a task to metabolize it — he just finishes the line because it's his job, and the closest thing to a 'task' (asking to move to mornings) he explicitly denies is about the fear. This suggests the mechanism may be more about domestic/relational grief specifically than fear in general.

evidence.quote: When there's a task you can do you do it and then you're not standing in a kitchen looking at a light.
I started writing things down, times, money, what needed paying.

candidates.falsifier: If in a moment of clear fear or grief he sat with the feeling and named it directly instead of pivoting to a logistical detail, this would weaken the claim.
candidates.would_predict: Work and Career: under financial stress he will respond by creating a tracking system (a ledger, an envelope, a spreadsheet) before or instead of discussing the stress with anyone.

candidates.headline: He will absorb financial or physical cost silently to protect someone else's dignity or safety, and treats being caught doing so as a failure of the act itself.
candidates.explanation: He secretly sent Simone money for a year and let his mother insult her rather than admit it (E2, 'if I said no, Mother, actually I'm the one sending, she'd want to know with what money'); he gave his whole paycheck to a stroke victim's family and lied to his six-year-old that he'd eaten (E3); he chose to skip his own envelope savings and eat badly for three weeks rather than touch Bete's fund (E5). In each case the value is not generosity in the abstract but generosity that must remain undetected — being seen giving would apparently compromise it or expose him to correction.
candidates.narrator_frame: He calls the sofa-lie 'not nobility' (E2 L49) and the cracker-lie 'stupid — not stupid, I don't regret it' (E3 L49), actively resisting a heroic frame even as he reports the same concealment pattern three times.
candidates.form_evidence: Precision markers cluster around the cost, not the act: 'a hundred, hundred and fifty,' 'all of it,' 'three weeks' — but the concealment itself is described in vague, almost embarrassed shorthand ('I let her say it,' 'I told everyone I sold it'), suggesting the hiding is the part he's least comfortable narrating.
candidates.check: E2: hides remittances behind the sofa story. E3: hides the empty stomach behind 'I ate at the garage.' E5: hides the financial strain of not touching the envelope ('I ate badly instead for three weeks. Which is stupid.'). E1 and E4 do not feature this concealment mechanism.
candidates.counterexample: In E5 he is not hiding the envelope's existence from Bete — she knows there was money 'since she was about eleven' presumably, though this isn't confirmed; if she does know about the envelope, the concealment is only of his own suffering (going hungry), not of the giving itself, which is a narrower claim than the other two cases.

evidence.quote: the answer was I stopped paying the installments on the sofa and the store came and took the sofa and I told everyone I sold it.

candidates.falsifier: An instance where he gave help openly and let the recipient or family know the true cost to him, without constructing a cover story.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: in a future partnership or close friendship, he will underreport his own sacrifices or debts, and a partner will discover a hidden financial or physical cost only by accident, not disclosure.

candidates.headline: Under acute threat he defaults to slow, verbal de-escalation anchored in ordinary human detail, and this is what people specifically seek him out for afterward.
candidates.explanation: Facing an armed, shaking teenager, his instinct was not silence or compliance alone but active conversation — asking where he was going, offering a personal connection ('my cousin lived in Grajaú') — while simultaneously running tactical calculations (headcount, keeping the confrontation at the front of the bus). This is a distinct capability from the caretaking/logistics value seen elsewhere: it's read-the-room-and-talk-a-stranger-down under real danger, and the supervisor's reaction (hand on his neck, offering him the next day off) signals this is recognized by others as exceptional, not just adequate.
candidates.narrator_frame: He downplays it as accidental and almost comic: 'I don't even remember what about, honestly... which is a comedy, right, I'm being robbed and I'm asking about his destination like a taxi' (L24-26) — he does not claim skill, he claims luck or absurdity.
candidates.form_evidence: The only place in the corpus where he narrates real-time tactical thinking with this density ('the entire thought in my head was: if this goes bad it has to go bad at the front. Not back there') — the specificity of threat-management reasoning appears nowhere else, suggesting this is a genuinely activated, not habitual, capacity.
candidates.check: n/a — single experience, not a cross-experience frequency claim.
candidates.counterexample: He also credits the boy's own hesitation and the fact he 'never done this' for the safe outcome, which could mean the de-escalation worked because the threat was soft, not because of his skill — the counterfactual (a hardened robber) is untested in the corpus.

evidence.quote: So I kept driving. And I talked to him... And he kept the knife there but he started answering me.
Seu Aparecido... he looked at the bus and he looked at me and he said, Edilson, and he put his hand on the back of my neck

candidates.falsifier: If he described freezing, staying silent, or complying wordlessly in a comparable high-stakes confrontation elsewhere in the corpus, this would weaken the claim that verbal de-escalation is his default mode under threat.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: Communication and conflict — in a heated argument with a family member, he will be observed to slow the pace and introduce an unrelated, humanizing detail (a memory, a joke, a question about something mundane) rather than confronting the conflict head-on.

candidates.headline: He says he wants Bete to leave and go far, but when a real chance to leave appears he quietly blocks it and then narrates his own sabotage without softening it.
candidates.explanation: He repeats the aspiration ('I want her to go far... I want her in Campinas,' E5 L31) as a stated identity, but when the Santa Catarina exchange came up, he 'found reasons' — food, cold, company — and she dropped it. This is not simple hypocrisy; the interesting gap is that he sees it clearly and names it without excuse ('I know exactly what I did and I did it anyway'), meaning the contradiction is conscious, not self-deceived, which raises the question of what the professed value ('going far') is actually protecting him from if he abandons it under real pressure.
candidates.narrator_frame: He explicitly flags the contradiction himself: 'And I know exactly what I did and I did it anyway. So, you know. Man of God, fifteen years, still an idiot on a Tuesday' (L38-40) — he names the gap but frames it as a moral failing/joke rather than investigating the fear underneath (losing her, after having already lost a brother and a partner to sudden absence).
candidates.form_evidence: The vagueness spike ('I found a lot of reasons... the food would be different, the cold, who would she be with') contrasts with his usual hyper-precision (bus times, distances, money amounts) — when the real motive is protecting his own attachment, the specificity that marks his honesty elsewhere disappears.
candidates.check: Single clear instance in E5; the 'wanting her to leave' aspiration is repeated multiple times in E5 (L31, L33) but only tested once against a concrete opportunity, so this is a within-experience pattern (stated repeatedly vs. acted on once) rather than a multi-experience frequency claim.
candidates.counterexample: He does support her daily commute to a school an hour away and gives her the two extra minutes for the safer route, which is a real instance of enabling her independence and mobility — the sabotage is specific to prolonged distance/separation, not to autonomy in general, so the claim should be scoped to distance, not to control broadly.

evidence.quote: I say it at church, I say, my daughter's going to university, she's going to leave this place, I want her in Campinas
I found a lot of reasons. The food would be different, the cold, who would she be with, and she looked at me for a long time and then she said okay, Dad, fine

candidates.falsifier: If he later actively supported a similar or larger separation opportunity for Bete (a full move away, a longer program), this specific block would look like a one-off rather than a protective mechanism tied to loss.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: Family and parenting — when Bete applies to university outside São Paulo, he will express verbal support publicly while raising a series of practical objections privately before the decision is finalized.

candidates.headline: He counts people obsessively in moments of responsibility for others' safety, a habit that started as grief-arithmetic and became operational vigilance.
candidates.explanation: At seventeen he compulsively recalculated Wellington's ambulance route and timing down to the minute ('I knew every route... Seven minutes,' E1 L35-41) despite having no power to act on it. Decades later as a bus driver he counts passengers as a functional habit during the robbery ('there were eleven people on that bus. I counted, I always count, that's a habit,' E4 L30-31). The throughline is that numeric tracking of people/time is how he manages helplessness — it started as a useless post-hoc ritual after a death he couldn't prevent, and became a genuinely useful professional reflex, but the underlying drive (control via counting, in situations where the outcome is actually out of his hands) is the same.
candidates.narrator_frame: In E4 he frames the counting as pure professional habit ('that's a habit') with no acknowledgment of its origin or resemblance to the ambulance-math in E1; the two are never connected by him.
candidates.form_evidence: Numeric precision is the most distinctive form marker in the whole corpus (fifty-one minutes, seven minutes, eleven people, three old, eighty meters, four forty, thirty reais) and it clusters specifically around scenes of danger or loss, not around neutral scenes (church, e.g., is comparatively number-free apart from durations of years).
candidates.check: E1: counts/recalculates ambulance route minutes. E2: counts money amounts precisely (a hundred, hundred fifty) but not people. E3: minimal counting, more sensory/duration description. E4: explicitly counts passengers as a stated habit. E5: counts minutes of the walking route (seven, nine, two more minutes) obsessively.
candidates.counterexample: E3 breaks the pattern most: in the scene of most acute emotional exposure (near-crisis at Bete's bedside, thoughts 'that I don't think came from the Lord'), there is no numeric counting at all — he shifts instead to sensory description ('it sounds like a river'), suggesting the counting mechanism is specifically tied to scenarios involving transit/physical danger, not general distress.

evidence.quote: I knew every route. I knew you could take Estrada do Campo Limpo but if there's the market on Sunday you cut behind the school.
there were eleven people on that bus. I counted, I always count, that's a habit, you count the heads at each stop.

candidates.falsifier: If he described a comparable danger scenario (not transit-related) where he did not resort to counting or timing, this would narrow the claim to transit-specific vigilance rather than a general grief-to-control mechanism.
candidates.would_predict: Health and Wellness: when a family member is sick or hospitalized, he will track and recite precise timings (wait times, dosage schedules, appointment counts) as his primary way of engaging with the situation.

candidates.headline: He values being asked for nothing so highly that he identifies it as the single thing that made a spiritual authority trustworthy.
candidates.explanation: Of everything he could praise about Bené and Pastor Almir, what he foregrounds is their restraint: Bené 'never once asked me about Simone. Not one time in five years' (E3 L24-25), and of Almir, 'I never asked him for anything. Not once' is reciprocally matched by the pastor's habit of asking without pushing. The cost is that this is presented as the reason he trusted them enough to be reachable at his lowest point — meaning his capacity for trust is conditioned on the other person not extracting disclosure, which is a specific and costly value: it means he is most reachable by people who make the fewest emotional demands of him.
candidates.narrator_frame: He frames this warmly as why the relationship worked ('I think because he didn't ask me anything') rather than examining what it implies about his own guardedness.
candidates.form_evidence: The repetition and emphasis ('Not one time in five years', 'Not once') function as evidence of how closely he tracked the absence of being asked — he is keeping score of what was not demanded of him, which itself is a form of vigilance around exposure.
candidates.counterexample: In the same experience he does eventually give generously and vulnerably (the entire paycheck to the stroke victim's family) without being asked, which shows the guardedness is specific to being asked about his own inner state, not to generosity or connection generally.

evidence.quote: He never once asked me about Simone. Not one time in five years.
I never asked him for anything. Not once.

candidates.falsifier: If he described a relationship where direct questioning about his feelings led to trust or relief rather than avoidance, this value claim would weaken.
candidates.would_predict: Relationships: Friendships and community — in new friendships he will gravitate toward people who do not probe his personal life, and will describe feeling closest to those who simply show up rather than ask questions.

candidates.headline: He notices other people's small, private rituals for holding themselves together (nails, shoe-cleaning, hall lights) far more precisely than he names his own.
candidates.explanation: He remembers Wellington's toothbrush-cleaned shoes in forensic detail (E1 L45-46), reinterprets Simone's nightly manicure years later as her one act of self-possession (E2 L17-22), and notices Bete leaving the hall light on for him (E5 L57). In each case the ritual belongs to someone else, and he reads it with unusual empathy — but he doesn't apply the same lens to his own compulsive routines (rerouting, counting, timing routes), which he frames as logistics rather than as his own version of the same self-holding behavior.
candidates.narrator_frame: He explicitly reframes Simone's nails after the fact ('I understand it now... at the time I thought she was vain,' E2 L20-22), showing he's capable of this reinterpretation in hindsight — but does not turn that same retrospective lens on his own habits within these accounts.
candidates.form_evidence: The sensory specificity he gives to other people's rituals (the toothbrush, the little white line, the hall light 'because of the bill') is not applied with equal warmth to his own rituals, which are narrated in logistical, justifying language (route times, cost comparisons) rather than emotional ones.
candidates.check: E1: Wellington's shoes. E2: Simone's nails. E5: Bete's hall light. E3 and E4 do not feature this specific noticing-another's-ritual pattern as clearly, though E3's 'everything's resolved' becoming Bete's joke is adjacent.
candidates.counterexample: His own '4am at the church, sleeping in the plastic chair' (E3) could be read as him allowing himself a ritual and later naming it as such ('that was the most rest I got') — this is a case where he does apply warmth to his own routine, weakening the claim that he never does this for himself.

evidence.quote: the shoes were in there and they were so clean. He cleaned them with a toothbrush, that guy, every night

patterns_identified.title: Silent absorption of cost to protect another's dignity
patterns_identified.description: Willingly sacrifices and conceals the sacrifice to prevent someone else from knowing the cost, with emphasis on the concealment rather than the generosity
